paras: The burning of the Smith and Brisco store was the destruction by fire of a store owned by two Black men, Israel Smith and Hansom Brisco, eight or ten miles southeast of Colfax in Grant Parish, Louisiana, on the night of December 9, 1880. No one was hurt, but the local paper first described it as an attack by armed "incendiaries" and then, a week later, reported a rumor that the owners had burned the store themselves for the insurance.

The store stood on Bayou Philip or Bayou Darro, "in a lonely spot in the woods," and dealt in seed cotton. According to the Colfax Chronicle, a dozen white men had been in the same seed-cotton business all fall, and Smith and Brisco were "only following the lead" of them. The paper also wrote that a young Black man had been killed in the same store early in the fall by men shooting through its walls.

At about ten o'clock on Thursday night, unknown persons set fire to the store and burned it to the ground. While it burned, several volleys were fired into it. No one was inside, since the occupants were at a house several hundred yards away and, in the paper's words, "too frightened to venture near." The Chronicle put the loss at nearly $800 in goods and about $100 for the building.

Smith told the paper he had no clue whether the attackers were white or Black. The Chronicle called for "active operations" against what it called a "nest of outlaws," but no report of an arrest or investigation appears in the coverage.

The Colfax Chronicle first ran the story under the headline "Murderous Incendiaries," saying the attackers deserved "a term in the penitentiary or justice at the end of a limb" and that "These negroes are entitled to protection." It guessed the motive was "to strike a blow at the 'seed cotton' traffic," adding that it was "a poor beginning" to start with "a couple of timid negroes."

A week later, under "Another Version," the same paper wrote that "In justice to our people" it would report the "common report" that the owners had burned the store for the insurance and fired guns to give it "the color of an 'outrage.'" It judged this version as probable as the first. The Donaldsonville Chief reprinted a shortened version of the first report, credited to the "Grant Chronicle," in its state-news summary of December 25, without the later retraction.

The coverage leaves open who set the fire: the Chronicle's first account blamed an outside band, while its second account, resting on unattributed rumor, blamed the owners, and no later report settling the question was found.

reader.title: Burning of the Smith and Brisco store, Grant Parish, Louisiana
bases: The only reported acts are burning a store and firing volleys into it while it was empty, by an unidentified party, and a week later the same paper reported a rumor that the owners set the fire themselves (A2, A3).

There is only one independent source, the Colfax Chronicle (the Donaldsonville Chief reprinted it), and its own follow-up gave the 'common report' that the owners burned the store for the insurance, calling that version as probable as the first (A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle, first report
accounts.gist: A band of 'cut-throats' burned the two Black men's store and fired volleys into it, probably to strike at the 'seed cotton' traffic; the paper said they were the same men who had killed a young man in the store in the fall.

accounts.label: Israel Smith
accounts.gist: Smith said he had no clue whether the attackers were white or Black men.

accounts.label: 'Common report' (Colfax Chronicle follow-up)
accounts.gist: The owners themselves had a hand in burning the store for the insurance and fired guns to give it the color of an 'outrage'; the paper said this was as probable as its first account.

framing.detail: Under 'Murderous Incendiaries' the Chronicle called for the attackers to get 'the penitentiary or justice at the end of a limb' and said the 'timid negroes' deserved protection, then a week later under 'Another Version' it printed the insurance-fraud rumor 'In justice to our people.'
The Donaldsonville Chief ran an abridged version of the condemnatory first report in its 'Summary of State News' and did not carry the follow-up.

versions.value: An outside band of 'cut-throats', the same set who killed a young man in the store in the fall, aiming at the seed-cotton traffic
The owners themselves, burning the store for the insurance and firing guns to fake an 'outrage' ('common report')

conflicts.note: Both versions come from the same paper, a week apart; the second rests on unattributed 'common report' and the paper called the two equally probable. No later report settles it.
The local paper's spelling is likely the original; the Chief reprinted it.
